newsitem.title: UK: ITN sees IRA truce but sources sceptical.
newsitem.headline: ITN sees IRA truce but sources sceptical.

text.p: Britain's ITN television said on Tuesday that Northern Ireland's IRA guerrillas would call a truce in the next few days, ahead of the British general election on May 1.
But Irish republican sources were sceptical of the report, which they said did not appear to reflect current Irish Republican Army thinking. "That's news to me," said one such source.

The sources said the IRA had repeatedly said it would only call a new truce if Britain invited its political wing, Sinn Fein to Belfast peace talks without preconditions and within an agreed and fixed time frame.
They said they could not rule out the possibility of an undeclared truce which would ease tension in the province while Sinn Fein campaigns for the election.
It is contesting several seats and says it is likely to win as many of two but will not take places in the London parliament because it would imply allegiance to Britain.

The IRA has attacked British targets and security forces in Northern Ireland with increasing intensity in recent weeks and said in an Easter statement that it would keep battling until Ireland was united.

Britain says the IRA, which is fighting British rule of the province, can only take part when there is a complete and verifiable end to its 28-year campaign and the guerrillas show willing to abandon violence and their arms for good.
ITN quoted security sources as saying the truce, which would be limited to a period of a few weeks before and after the election, may not be publicly declared.

Reports of a possible IRA truce have surfaced several times in recent weeks in the build-up to British elections which are likely to result in the opposition Labour party deposing Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government.

Labour's opposition spokeswoman, Mo Mowlam, said at the weekend that Sinn Fein could be at the Belfast peace talks if the IRA called a truce now which could be verified before the negotiations resume on June 3.
The Conservative party has said almost the same but has taken a tough public stand on the need for the IRA to break with violence altogether.
